### H-5 STABILITY OF DISCRETE-TIME SYSTEMS

The definitions of BIBO and zero-input stability can be readily extended to linear time-invariant SISO discrete-data control systems.

#### H-5-1 BIBO Stability

Let \( u(kT) \), \( y(kT) \), and \( g(kT) \) be the input, output, and impulse sequence of a linear time-invariant SISO discrete-data system, respectively. With zero initial conditions, the system is said to be BIBO stable, or simply stable, if its output sequence \( y(kT) \) is bounded to a bounded input \( u(kT) \). As with the treatment in Section 2-8, we can show that, for the system to be BIBO stable, the following condition must be met:

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} |g(kT)| < \infty \tag{H-157}
\]

#### H-5-2 Zero-Input Stability

For zero-input stability, the output sequence of the system must satisfy the following conditions:

\[
|y(kT)| \leq M < \infty \tag{H-158}
\]
\[
\lim_{k \to \infty} |y(kT)| = 0 \tag{H-159}
\]

Thus, zero-input stability can also be referred to as **asymptotic stability**. We can show that both the BIBO stability and the zero-input stability of discrete-data systems require that the roots of the characteristic equation lie inside the unit circle \( |z| = 1 \) in the z-plane.

This is not surprising, because the \( j\omega \)-axis of the s-plane is mapped onto the unit circle in the z-plane. The regions of stability and instability for discrete-data systems in the z-plane are shown in Fig. H-17. Let the characteristic equation roots of a linear discrete-data time-invariant SISO system be \( z_i \), \( i = 1, 2, \ldots, n \). The possible stability conditions of the system are summarized in Table H-2 with respect to the roots of the characteristic equation.

\[K = [k_{1} \ k_{2} ]\]

Applying the SFG gain formula to Fig. H-56(b), with \(X_{1}(s)\) and \(X_{2}(s)\) as outputs and \(x_{1}(kT)\) and \(x_{2}(kT)\) as inputs, we have

\[X_{2}(s) = \frac{-2500k_{1}}{s(s+25)} x_{1}(kT) - \frac{2500k_{2}}{s(s+25)} x_{2}(kT) + \frac{1}{s+25} x_{2}(kT)\] (H-305)

Taking the inverse Laplace transform on both sides of Eqs. (H-305) and (H-306) and letting \(t = (k + 1)T\), we have the discrete-data state equations as

x_{1}[(k + 1)T] &= (1 - 0.1152k_{1})x_{1}(kT) + (0.2212 - 0.1152k_{2})x_2(kT)\\

\end{align*}\]

Thus, the coefficient matrix of the closed-loop system with state feedback is

initial conditions (a) to (c) are integral equations that approximate kernel deformation in a Gaussian process model. The first series (work by Evans et al.) incrementally builds up the kernel by first using a Sobolev kernel convolution and then by multiplying this kernel by a random function sampled from a mean-zero GP process conditioned on a fixed output y. The second series (work by Joner and West) takes the first series approximation and generates kernels directly from projections of the φ function on a finite grid, again using a Sobolev kernel convolution. The third series (the authors' development) uses the first two series and introduces a family of norms for specifying the kernel during the generation process. The fourth series (represented by the Stoyan group) uses kernels constructed using a commonly used orthonormal series (Green et al.) and produces properties appropriate to hydraulic conductivity. The fifth series (developed by Wu and colleagues) uses a Schauder framework.

While there are many other papers on this calculus—from Hytönen (2000) to Jones (2000) to Pearl (1988)—these papers were of help in connecting the theory they developed in this thesis to what was known about continuous data. This illustrates how new sampling schemes for temporal data (and data from other domains) ought to be a source of new insights into the development of stochastic models, even if the underlying mechanisms remain unaltered.

While the models and programming methods here are all discrete in nature, the underlying concepts (e.g., about processes viewed by stochastic transformations) are ordered on the theory and practice subfields (e.g., [18], [29]) that also use these concepts as the basis for functioning systems. And while these same subfields with respect to this theory are fairly small, several important tools and technical objects of the subject have been established there. These include sequences of independent multivariate standard normal random variables, their Bhongalev–Bhuyan interleaving and mixture variants, Newton–Cotes quadrature, interval transforms, and others.

This work can be loosely classified as (1) development of a calculus and associated theory for continuous data, which in principle can be used as the basis for a number of stochastic models, especially in applications involving large data sets and models themselves, (2) correlation and related theoretical analyses, (3) bootstrap techniques for the model, and (4) applications of the more general theories to other strategies, including sensitivity analysis and other approaches to robustifying models. It is also expected that future work will incorporate higher-order statistics as the theoretical framework strengthens. Some of this work in process modeling is already standard and formal in form, at least in microcosm as the result of informal discussions and exchanges.
